report.source_text: On evaluation, marked periocular and facial swelling was easily appreciated. Palpation of the involved area revealed crepitus consistent with subcutaneous emphysema, and there was 2.5-mm relative proptosis by the Hertel exophthalmometry. There was no other evidence of infectious cellulitis: the involved area was not erythematous, warm, or tender.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 79-year-old man with a history of hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation, Parkinson's disease, hepatitis, and peripheral vascular disease underwent replacement of loose mandibular denture-anchoring implants with a zygomatic implant. Six days after the procedure, he presented with acute-onset painless swelling around the left eye and cheek. Physical examination revealed marked periocular and facial swelling with crepitus on palpation consistent with subcutaneous emphysema and 2.5-mm relative proptosis by Hertel exophthalmometry. There were no signs of infectious cellulitis. Ophthalmologic examination showed preserved visual acuity (20/30 OU), normal intraocular pressures (14 and 12 mmHg), symmetric pupils with normal reactivity, and normal extraocular motility, ruling out orbital compartment syndrome. CT imaging of the orbits and paranasal sinuses confirmed the presence of subcutaneous air extending into the left periocular area and orbit, with a defect in the left maxillary wall adjacent to the dental implant, identifying the source of air entry. The patient was observed closely without intervention, and the subcutaneous emphysema and proptosis resolved spontaneously with time.
